Although Alien: Isolation has been out for nearly 2 years, I just recently finished it and thought I'd share a review. I played it on a PC built for gaming using a controller. If you have a system that can support maximum settings I'd also recommend modifying the settings file to increase pop-in distance and increase the shadow map resolution (see this link).

TL;DR: somewhat disappointing, especially considering it won several "game of the year" awards.

The good: scenery throughout this game is fantastic. It looks and sounds quite good from start to finish, and, at least initially, sets the stage well for an entry to the survival horror genre. The first several encounters with the alien are particularly tense, as its AI was designed so as to be somewhat unpredictable (played on "medium" difficulty setting); just as soon as you think it might be headed in the other direction, it's likely to turn around and obstruct your intended path again. There are many frenzied moments in which the alien unexpectedly (re)appears and the player must quickly but quietly hide or cause a distraction, lest the alien spear the protagonist, Amanda Ripley (daughter of the films' hero) with its tail, or bite off her face. At least initially, the alien's behavior compels one to carefully creep around corners or duck into the nearest locker when the creature is nearby, and successfully maintains the feeling that Ripley is vulnerable, even after she gains access to certain defensive measures. Even if/when Ripley meets an untimely demise, there are enough save points scattered throughout so as to minimize the amount of tiresome repetition of tricky segments.

The bad: Once the player becomes accustomed to the flow of the game, Alien: Isolation feels like an elaborated walking (or, more often, crouching) simulator with very limited FPS elements (again, played on medium difficulty). The motion sensor, which the player acquires very early in the game, allows Ripley to easily bypass most inhabitants of the space station Sevastopol in many circumstances (unlike the alien, other hostiles seem to follow a set path). Additionally, the same motion tracker can be used to navigate to the next objective throughout, as it provides turn-by-turn directions in an overwhelming majority of situations. It's very easy to lean on the motion tracker's directions and beeline from one objective to the next; sadly, the majority of most missions boil down to something like the following:

1) sneak through dark space station corridors, avoiding hostiles;

2) find the door/other objective you need to access;

3) backtrack across the map to power up a generator, because power to the door/objective has failed

4) repeat

All of this goes on far, far too long.

The ugly: To the extent it exists, the story in Alien: Isolation is extremely sparse. The opening sequence starts off well enough, with Ripley given an opportunity to discover the fate of her mother; however, it plummets precipitously and immediately from there. After the first few missions, the story devolves into, "get out of this perilous situation and into yet another". While the voice actor for Ripley is quite good, her character barely evolves past surviving one scrape after another. There are interesting bits of the story throughout which are never fully developed; during the second half, in particular, it seems as if the writers just decided to phone in a totally mediocre plot which is just good enough to support the gameplay. Having finished the game, I'd also argue there is almost no reason to play through it again, even on a harder difficulty.

If you enjoy survival horror games, I'd definitely recommend SOMA over Alien: Isolation; while the former could also be fairly criticized as an elaborated walking-simulator, SOMA's puzzles and story are orders of magnitude superior to Alien: Isolation, and it's a hell of a lot creepier as well.
